headline: Three commercial AI systems flagged signs of breast cancer on mammograms up to six years before diagnosis in about one in five cases, a Swedish study in the journal Radiology found.
score_reason: Pool score 5, lowered by 2: the study was released on 9 Jun 2026, four months ago, and the new element is only an expert comment in an Italian outlet.
importance_line: Women who attend breast screening could one day be offered closer follow-up based on AI scores, but this looked back at old scans of women already diagnosed and no benefit for women has been shown.
summary: Il Sole 24 ORE reports on a Swedish study in the journal Radiology, first released by the Radiological Society of North America on 9 Jun 2026, in which three commercially available AI systems scored 88,963 mammograms from 31,394 patients and, at 90% specificity (correctly clearing cancer-free cases), flagged up to 19.7% of those later diagnosed with breast cancer six years before diagnosis and up to 39.3% two years before. Study leader Fredrik Strand of Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm calls it a sign of AI's potential, but Massimo Calabrese, director of the oncology and breast radiology unit at Policlinico San Martino in Genoa, warns that finding such signs in old scans is not the same as diagnosing a tumour six years earlier and that real benefit for women still has to be shown.
notes: OLDER NEWS RE-DATED: the RSNA release (rsna.org/media/press/2026/2658; EurekAlert and News-Medical show the same 9 Jun 2026 date) already announced this study; Il Sole 24 ORE's English edition carried it on 13 Oct 2026 with a new Italian expert comment. A '38.5 per cent diagnosed' figure appears in both texts but looks odd for a screening population, so it is left out.
